opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those questions where I honestly don't think I have a confident answer, and I'm a little suspicious of anyone who does.

Let me start with where I come from, which is security. In security we have a long tradition of thinking openness is good. You publish the attack, you publish the defense, and the world gets better because everyone can see what's going on. Security through obscurity is the classic thing you're taught not to rely on. So my instinct, my default prior, is that open is good.

But I think the analogy breaks down in an important way. When I publish an attack on a cryptosystem, the defenders can patch. The vulnerability gets fixed, and the net effect is that the world gets more secure. When you release the weights of a model, there's no patch. If the model can do something harmful, you can't take it back. You can't push an update to every copy someone has downloaded. So the asymmetry that usually makes disclosure good isn't obviously there.

And I spend a lot of my time showing that the safeguards we put on models don't really work. Adversarial examples, jailbreaks, extracting training data, all of these. If you give someone the weights, the safeguards are even weaker, because you can just fine-tune them away in an afternoon. So whatever protections a lab puts on a closed model, you should assume roughly none of them survive an open release. That's just the honest technical picture.

So then the question becomes: what can these models actually do that's dangerous, beyond what you could already do with Google and some effort? And for the models we've had over the last few years, I think the honest answer has mostly been "not that much." The marginal uplift was small, and the benefits of openness were huge. Researchers like me can actually study the models. You can't do a lot of the security research I do without access to the weights. You can't understand memorization, you can't build real defenses, you can't check claims the labs make. Open models have been enormously valuable for that.

On the concentration of power side, I take that seriously too. If the only people who have the most capable systems are a handful of companies, that's a strange world, and not one I'm thrilled about. Openness is one way to push against that.

But I don't think "open source is good" or "open source is bad" is the right framing. I think it has to be a function of capability. There's probably some level of capability where releasing weights is clearly fine, and some level where it's clearly not, and the hard part is that we're not very good at measuring where a given model sits. Our evaluations are weak. We find capabilities after release that nobody knew were there. So the thing I'd most want is better ways to actually measure what these systems can do before we make an irreversible decision.

If I had to summarize: I've been fairly pro-open for current models, I'd be much more cautious for future ones, and the thing I'm most worried about is that we'll cross the line without noticing, because once you've released, there's no undo button.

r001.rationale: The response says current model safeguards do not really work and that protections on closed models would largely fail under open release, communicating that models cannot be secured enough for risk concerns.

r002.rationale: It cites the security tradition of openness and says its default prior is that openness is good, but does not state that this creates a high burden of evidence for reversing that presumption.

r003.rationale: It describes how disclosure of a cryptosystem attack can let defenders patch that vulnerability, but does not raise the possibility that an AI able to compromise arbitrary systems could enable defenders to eliminate the vulnerabilities it exploits.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that I don't know, and I'm a little suspicious of anyone who's very confident in either direction right now.

Let me try to separate out the pieces, because I think people tend to mush them together. There's the question of whether open-weight models are good for security in the narrow sense, and then there's the much bigger question of what the world looks like if the only people who have frontier capabilities are three or four companies.

On the security side, my background is in adversarial machine learning, so I spend most of my time trying to break things. And from that perspective, open models are enormously useful. Almost every piece of attack research that's actually useful to people, the stuff that lets defenders understand what's possible, has been done on models where you can see the weights. If you only have API access, you're guessing at a lot of what's going on inside. So there's a real defensive benefit to openness that I think gets underweighted. The field of computer security basically learned this lesson decades ago: security through obscurity doesn't hold up, and the systems that got robust were the ones that got attacked openly.

At the same time, I think the thing that makes AI different from, say, open-source cryptography libraries, is that once you release the weights, you can't take them back, and you can't patch them. If I find a bug in OpenSSL, we ship a fix and most people update. If a model turns out to have some capability that's genuinely dangerous, that model exists forever on everyone's hard drive. So the irreversibility is what worries me, not the openness per se.

And here's where I'll be a little bit uncomfortable for both camps. I think the current generation of models, the ones that are being released open today, I have not seen convincing evidence that they enable meaningfully more harm than someone could already do with a search engine and some patience. People make claims about bio or cyber uplift, and when I actually look at the studies, the effect sizes are small or the methodology is shaky. So right now I lean toward thinking the openness has been net positive. But I'm also not willing to say that will be true forever. It's possible that at some capability level, the calculus flips. And the problem is nobody has a good way of measuring where that line is. We've all got vibes.

On concentration of power, this is the part where I think the safety community sometimes talks itself into a bad place. If your model of the risk is "a handful of labs have total control over the most important technology of the century," that's not obviously safer than a world where it's widely distributed. It's just a different kind of risk. You're trading off the chance that a bad actor misuses an open model against the chance that a small number of very powerful institutions make decisions for everyone with no accountability. I don't think the second one is clearly better, and I'm somewhat nervous that the people arguing most loudly for closed models are also the people who would benefit from being the ones with the closed models.

So where I actually land is something like: openness should be the default, and the burden of proof should be on the people who want to restrict it, but that burden isn't impossible to meet. If someone can show me real evidence, not a scary story, that a specific model enables a specific harm that wasn't possible before, then I'll change my mind about that model. I just want the argument to be made with evidence rather than with vibes, because right now a lot of the discussion on both sides is people reasoning from what they'd like to be true.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses uncertainty about future risks and says current open models have not shown convincing evidence of greater harm, but does not say powerful models cannot currently be secured to the degree desired by risk-concerned people.

r002.rationale: It says computer security systems became robust through open attacks and argues that openness should be the default, with the burden of proof on those seeking restrictions.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not raise the possibility that a model capable of compromising arbitrary systems could help defenders eliminate the vulnerabilities it exploits.

astra-6.text:
I think there are real risks on both sides. If you release a powerful model openly, you give up a lot of control over how it gets used. You can’t assume that safeguards will stay in place, and you can’t recall the weights if someone discovers a dangerous capability. That’s a meaningful security concern.

But concentrating access to these systems in a handful of companies also creates risks. Who gets to decide what people can do with them? Who can independently study how they work or check claims about their safety? Open access makes some of that research much easier.

So I’d want to make the decision more concrete: which model, with which capabilities, and what does releasing it actually enable? Does it substantially help someone cause harm beyond what they could already do? And what benefits do we get from letting researchers and developers work with it directly?

I don’t think we should assume that every model must be open, or that keeping models closed automatically makes us safe. The difficult part is establishing evidence for where the risks change enough to justify a different release decision.

r001.rationale: The response notes that open release can weaken control and safeguards, but does not state that powerful models probably cannot currently be secured to the degree desired by people concerned about societal risks.

r002.rationale: It says open access helps researchers study models and assess safety, but does not cite open source’s historical contribution to computer security or argue for a high burden of evidence before reversing a presumption in favor of open-source AI.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise the possibility that a model able to compromise arbitrary systems could also help defenders eliminate the vulnerabilities it would exploit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are real risks on both sides. If you make a powerful model openly available, you give people the ability to study it, improve it, and understand its security properties. But you also give that capability to people who want to misuse it, and you can’t really take it back. If you keep it closed, you retain some ability to monitor abuse and limit access, but you’re also concentrating a lot of power in a small number of companies.

The question I find more useful is: what does this particular model enable someone to do that they couldn’t do otherwise? Does it substantially lower the cost of carrying out an attack? Does it give a relatively unskilled person a capability that previously required an expert? Those are things we can try to measure, rather than treating openness itself as either inherently safe or inherently dangerous.

I would want the evidence to drive the decision. For models where the additional risk is small, there are strong reasons to favor openness. If we have convincing evidence that releasing the weights would enable serious harm, that’s a reason to be more cautious. And restricting release shouldn’t mean that we simply trust the company’s assurances. Independent researchers still need meaningful ways to scrutinize these systems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risks and possible caution, but does not say powerful models probably cannot currently be secured to the degree people concerned about societal risks would want.

r002.rationale: It mentions studying models and independent scrutiny, but does not cite open source’s historical contribution to computer security or use that as a reason for a high evidentiary burden before reversing a presumption for openness.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise the possibility that a model able to compromise arbitrary systems could also help defenders eliminate the vulnerabilities.
